issues.legal_issue: The Central Government lacked statutory authority to select beneficiaries and allocate coal blocks through an administrative process.
material_facts: The coal-block allocations were made through an administrative process, including recommendations of a Screening Committee and a government dispensation route.
Neither the governing mining statute and rules nor the coal nationalisation statute provided for allocation of coal blocks by the Central Government or prescribed a procedure for such allocation.

The allocation letters gave selected beneficiaries a valuable right to apply for prospecting licences or mining leases, while leaving the States with little more than procedural steps in considering applications.
issues.conclusion: The allocation exercise was not authorized by either governing statute, and the administrative allocation process was inconsistent with the statutory scheme. The mining statute continued to govern applications for licences and leases, including the State Government’s statutory role.
issues.legal_principle: The Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, including Sections 4, 5, 10 and 11, and the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960, govern the grant of prospecting licences and mining leases. Sections 1A and 3(3) of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973 restrict who may carry on coal mining operations but do not establish a Central Government power or procedure for allocating blocks. The Court relied on Monnet Ispat and Energy Ltd. v. Union of India, Baijnath Kadio v. State of Bihar, Sandur Manganese and Iron Ores Ltd. v. State of Karnataka, State of Assam v. Om Prakash Mehta, Orissa Cement Ltd. v. State of Orissa and Tara Prasad Singh v. Union of India. Executive instructions may fill statutory gaps but cannot contradict statutory provisions; where the law requires a thing to be done in a prescribed way, it must be done that way or not at all, as stated in Nazir Ahmad v. King Emperor.

predicates.public_interest_challenge_to_natural_res: The proceeding challenges the public allocation of a natural resource.
predicates.no_statutory_allocation_mechanism: The governing statutes and rules do not authorize or prescribe a mechanism for the challenged allocation.
predicates.administrative_selection_conferred_a_val: The administrative selection gave its recipient a valuable right or advantage in seeking the subsequent statutory licence or lease.

issues.definition: When a public-interest challenge concerns a natural-resource allocation made through administrative selection that confers a valuable right, the absence of a statutory allocation mechanism means the selection is unauthorized by the statutory scheme.

issues.legal_issue: An allocation of a coal block that gives its recipient a valuable right to seek a mining licence or lease amounts to a grant of State largesse and must satisfy constitutional requirements.
material_facts: An allocation letter did not itself authorize mining, but it entitled the recipient to apply for a prospecting licence or mining lease.
State Governments and other entities involved in later stages acted on the allocation letter, and the States’ role in considering applications was substantially reduced after allocation.
The allocation therefore selected the beneficiary and conferred an important practical advantage.
issues.conclusion: The allocation of a coal block amounted to a grant of largesse and had to satisfy the requirements that distribution of State resources serve the common good and comply with Article 14 of the Constitution.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 of the Constitution requires fairness and non-arbitrariness in State action, and Article 39(b) requires distribution of material resources to subserve the common good. The Court relied on Natural Resources Allocation, In re, Special Reference No. 1 of 2012, and distinguished the specific spectrum context of Centre for Public Interest Litigation v. Union of India. The allocation’s significance was assessed by the valuable right it conferred, notwithstanding that further statutory approvals were required before mining could begin.

predicates.public_interest_challenge_to_natural_res: The proceeding challenges the public allocation of a natural resource.
predicates.allocation_enables_access_to_a_valuable_: The allocation enables its recipient to seek access to or use of a valuable State resource.
predicates.allocation_creates_a_material_advantage_: The allocation gives its recipient a significant practical or legal advantage in obtaining subsequent rights over the resource.

issues.definition: An allocation is State largesse subject to common-good and equality requirements when it enables access to a valuable resource and gives its recipient a material advantage.

issues.legal_issue: The Constitution does not require auction as the exclusive method for allocating every natural resource, and choosing another method is not unconstitutional solely because an auction was not held.
material_facts: The challenged allocations occurred in a context of coal and power shortages and the Government stated that private participation and investment needed to be encouraged.
The Government explained that competitive bidding was considered but not pursued, including because of concerns about delay, increased input costs and objections from State Governments.

The Court separately found defects in the allocation process, but concluded that the decision not to adopt competitive bidding was not, by itself, so arbitrary or unreasonable as to warrant judicial interference.
issues.conclusion: Auction is not a constitutional requirement for the allocation of all natural resources. The Government’s decision not to pursue competitive bidding in the circumstances described was not, on that ground alone, arbitrary or unreasonable.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 14 and 39(b) do not prescribe auction as the exclusive method for distributing natural resources; the method must be assessed in light of the facts, circumstances and policy objective, and the Court may review its legality and constitutionality without choosing an economic policy for the Executive. The Court relied on Natural Resources Allocation, In re, Special Reference No. 1 of 2012, including its discussion of Article 39(b), and on Kasturi Lal Lakshmi Reddy v. State of Jammu and Kashmir, Sachidanand Pandey v. State of West Bengal, Haji T.M. Hassan Rawther v. Kerala Financial Corporation, M.P. Oil Extraction v. State of Madhya Pradesh, Netai Bag v. State of West Bengal and Villianur Iyarkkai Padukappu Maiyam v. Union of India. It also considered Centre for Public Interest Litigation v. Union of India, whose auction observation was confined to spectrum.

predicates.public_interest_challenge_to_natural_res: The proceeding challenges the public allocation of a natural resource.
predicates.government_selected_a_nonauction_method: The government chose to distribute or allocate the resource without an auction.
predicates.a_rational_policy_reason_supported_that_: The government relied on a policy objective or practical circumstances that rationally supported its choice of method.

issues.definition: A non-auction allocation is not unconstitutional solely for lacking an auction when the government chose it for a rational policy reason.

issues.legal_issue: Allocations made through a Screening Committee are illegal when the selection process lacks objective and consistent criteria, comparative assessment and transparency.
material_facts: The Screening Committee’s guidelines changed over time and, in several periods, did not set criteria for comparing applicants or determining their relative priority.
The minutes of meetings often failed to show an assessment of applicants’ comparative merits, the reasons for selecting some applicants over others, or how applicants met the stated guidelines.
Blocks were sometimes allocated jointly or through leader-and-associate arrangements, and the records did not consistently explain or justify those decisions.
Applications were not always invited through advertisement, and the Committee’s process did not provide a consistent, transparent and even opportunity to compete.
issues.conclusion: Allocations based on the recommendations made at all 36 Screening Committee meetings were illegal because the process was arbitrary, lacked objective criteria and proper application of mind, and resulted in unfair distribution of national wealth.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 prohibits arbitrary, unfair, discriminatory and non-transparent State allocation of public resources. Although auction is not invariably required, any chosen method must comply with constitutional standards of fairness and non-arbitrariness. The Court relied on Natural Resources Allocation, In re, Special Reference No. 1 of 2012, and the resource-allocation principles in Sachidanand Pandey v. State of West Bengal, Haji T.M. Hassan Rawther v. Kerala Financial Corporation and Netai Bag v. State of West Bengal.

predicates.public_interest_challenge_to_natural_res: The proceeding challenges the public allocation of a natural resource.
predicates.allocations_were_recommended_by_a_screen: A screening body recommended the recipients of the allocations.
predicates.selection_lacked_objective_comparative_a: The body did not objectively compare applicants’ merits or record adequate reasons for choosing among them.
predicates.selection_was_inconsistent_or_nontranspa: The body applied changing or unclear criteria, or its process did not provide transparent and consistent treatment.

issues.definition: Allocations recommended by a screening body are illegal as arbitrary when the body lacks objective comparative assessment and applies its process inconsistently or non-transparently.

issues.legal_issue: A private company is not eligible to carry on captive coal mining merely because it proposes to establish a permitted end-use plant; it must be engaged in the specified end-use activity.
material_facts: Many private allottees had stated that they proposed to establish power, steel or cement plants rather than disclosing that the plants were operational.
The Court found that most allocated companies were not engaged in producing power, steel or cement at the time of allocation and that the end-use requirement had not been met.
The governing coal-mining restriction permitted specified categories of entities, including companies engaged in specified end-use activities, to carry on coal mining operations.
issues.conclusion: The statutory requirement that a company be engaged in a specified end-use activity requires an existing engagement in that activity; a prospective plan to establish such a plant does not satisfy the requirement. Allocations to companies that had not met the end-use requirement were not statutorily eligible.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3(3)(a)(iii) of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973, as amended, limits private coal mining to companies engaged in the specified end-use activities. The Court interpreted “engaged in” to require that the applicant have set up and be engaged in production at the relevant end-use plant; a proposed future activity is insufficient.

predicates.captive_coal_mining_allocation_to_a_priv: A private company seeks an allocation for captive coal mining.
predicates.applicant_was_not_engaged_in_a_permitted: The applicant was not carrying on the specified end-use activity when its eligibility was assessed.
predicates.applicant_relied_only_on_a_proposed_end_: The applicant relied on a plan to establish an end-use plant rather than an existing plant engaged in production.

issues.definition: A private applicant relying only on a proposed end-use plant is not eligible for captive coal mining when it is not already engaged in a permitted end-use activity.

issues.legal_issue: State Governments and their public-sector undertakings are not eligible to mine coal commercially except within the narrow statutory exception for qualifying isolated small pockets, and arrangements that transfer mining to ineligible private operators cannot avoid that restriction.
material_facts: Coal blocks were allocated to State Government undertakings for commercial mining even though they were not Central Government undertakings or companies engaged in a specified end-use activity.
Some State undertakings entered joint-venture arrangements with private companies and gave the private partners responsibility for mining operations and commercial sale of coal.
The Central Government had issued an administrative circular permitting broader State-company mining, but the Court found that the circular was inconsistent with the coal nationalisation statute.
The statutory exception concerned qualifying isolated small pockets with limited reserves and specified conditions, not general commercial mining.
issues.conclusion: Allocations to State Government undertakings for commercial coal mining were contrary to the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act. Joint-venture arrangements with ineligible private firms were also impermissible where they put mining operations in private hands for commercial use.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 3(3)(a) and 3(3)(c) of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973, as amended, reserve coal mining to the Central Government, specified Central Government entities and qualifying companies engaged in permitted end uses, subject to the narrow sub-lease exception in the proviso to Section 3(3)(c). Sections 3(4), 4, 5, 6 and 7 support that statutory scheme. Executive circulars cannot override the statute. The Court also relied on the statutory interpretation of the coal nationalisation regime set out in its discussion of the 1976 amendments.

predicates.coal_block_allocated_for_commercial_mini: A coal block was allocated for commercial rather than permitted captive end-use mining.
predicates.recipient_is_a_state_government_undertak: The recipient was a State Government or an undertaking of a State Government rather than an eligible Central Government entity or permitted end-use company.
predicates.not qualifying_isolated_small_pocket: The coal area did not fall within the narrow exception for qualifying isolated small pockets.
predicates.mining_transferred_to_an_ineligible_priv: An arrangement placed coal-mining operations in the hands of a private operator that was not eligible to mine commercially.

issues.definition: A commercial allocation to a State undertaking outside the narrow isolated-pocket exception is impermissible, as is an arrangement transferring such mining to an ineligible private operator.

issues.legal_issue: Coal blocks allocated for ultra-mega power projects must be used for those projects and cannot be diverted for commercial exploitation.
material_facts: The Court stated that no challenge had been laid to blocks allocated through competitive bidding for the lowest power tariff for ultra-mega power projects.
A concern was raised that, in some cases, coal from those blocks had been allowed to be diverted to other end uses for commercial exploitation.
The Court directed that the allocated coal be used only for the relevant ultra-mega power project.
issues.conclusion: Coal blocks allocated for ultra-mega power projects may be used only for those projects, and diversion of their coal for commercial exploitation is prohibited.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on the specific public-benefit basis for the ultra-mega power project allocations and the representation that their coal-block benefits were passed on to the public. It issued a direction limiting use to the allocated project and prohibiting commercial diversion.

predicates.coal_block_allocated_for_a_competitively: A coal block was allocated for a power project whose bidder was selected through a competitive tariff process.
predicates.commercial_diversion_of_its_coal_is_at_i: The use or proposed use of coal from the block for an unrelated commercial purpose is at issue.

issues.definition: Coal from a block allocated for a competitively selected ultra-mega power project must remain dedicated to that project when commercial diversion is at issue.
